title: Habit Tracker — Understanding Check
subtitle: 40 questions on the React + TypeScript habit tracker you built. Every question comes from your own code.

questions.prompt: Looking at the scripts in package.json, which command starts the local development server with hot reload?
options: npm run build
npm run preview
npm run dev
npm run lint

questions.prompt: The build script is "tsc -b && vite build". What does the tsc -b part do before Vite runs?
options: Type-checks the TypeScript project and fails the build if there are type errors
Installs any missing npm packages
Minifies the CSS output
Runs the ESLint rules

questions.prompt: Why is <App /> wrapped in <StrictMode> in main.tsx?
options: It makes the production bundle smaller
It is required for TypeScript to compile .tsx files
It stops users from opening the browser devtools
In development it runs extra checks and deliberately double-invokes certain functions to surface bugs

questions.prompt: In HabitList.tsx you render habits.map(habit => <HabitItem key={habit.id} ... />). Why does React need the key prop?
options: It sets the id attribute on the rendered HTML element
It tells React what order to sort the list in
It lets React match each item across renders so it can update and reorder the list correctly
It is required by TypeScript whenever you map over an array

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with using key={index} instead of key={habit.id} in that same list?
options: Nothing — index keys are always fine
When a habit is deleted from the middle, all the indices shift and React can end up associating DOM or state with the wrong habit
React throws a runtime error
The list would render in reverse order

questions.prompt: In HabitItem you have {streak !== 0 && 🔥 {streak}}. What appears on screen when streak is 0?
options: Nothing is rendered for that expression
The number 0 appears on screen
The word false appears on screen
React throws an error

questions.prompt: Suppose that same line had been written as {streak && 🔥 {streak}} — without the !== 0 check. What would show on screen when streak is 0?
options: The number 0 would be rendered on screen
undefined would render
Nothing would render
React would throw an error

questions.prompt: In App.tsx, <HabitProvider> wraps <Header />, <HabitForm /> and <HabitList />. What is it inside HabitProvider that makes those three components actually appear on the page?
options: HabitProvider renders its children prop
The useEffect inside App.tsx
React automatically renders anything nested inside any component
The key prop

questions.prompt: Button.tsx renders <button {...props} className={...} /> and never mentions children anywhere. So how does the text "Add Habit" still end up inside the button?
options: React automatically forwards any text it finds
children is just another prop, so it gets passed through by the {...props} spread
The Button component reads the text back out of the DOM
twMerge injects the text into the button

questions.prompt: In const [weekOffset, setWeekOffset] = useState(0), what is the [weekOffset, setWeekOffset] syntax doing?
options: Object destructuring
Array destructuring of the pair that useState returns
Using the spread operator
Declaring a TypeScript tuple type

questions.prompt: The Next button uses setWeekOffset(o => o + 1) rather than setWeekOffset(weekOffset + 1). Why prefer the function form?
options: It is required whenever the piece of state is a number
It is purely a style preference with no behavioural difference
It avoids triggering a re-render
It updates based on the latest queued state value, which stays correct even when React batches updates

questions.prompt: App.tsx recalculates visibleDates on every render from weekOffset, instead of storing it in its own useState. What is this approach called?
options: Derived state — computing a value from existing state instead of duplicating it in another useState
Prop drilling
A side effect
Memoization

questions.prompt: The input in HabitForm.tsx has both value={name} and onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)}. This makes it:
options: A controlled input, where React state is the single source of truth
An uncontrolled input
A ref-based input
A native HTML form action

questions.prompt: If you deleted value={name} from that input but kept the onChange handler, what would happen when setName("") runs after submitting?
options: The input would clear exactly as it does now
React would throw a warning and crash
The typed text would stay in the box, because the DOM is now holding the value instead of React
The form would submit a second time

questions.prompt: What does e.preventDefault() do at the top of handleSubmit?
options: It stops the click from bubbling up to parent elements
It prevents the browser's default form submission, which would reload the whole page
It stops the habit from being added twice
It prevents the input from being cleared

questions.prompt: deleteHabit is written as setHabits(curr => curr.filter(h => h.id !== id)). Why use filter instead of finding the index and calling curr.splice(i, 1)?
options: filter runs faster than splice
splice does not exist on arrays
filter returns a brand-new array, whereas splice mutates the existing state array in place and React can miss the change
filter also sorts the array for you

questions.prompt: In toggleHabit you return { ...h, completions } rather than doing h.completions = completions and returning h. Why does that matter?
options: Spread syntax is shorter to type
It produces a new habit object instead of mutating state, which is how React detects that something changed
It removes the old habit from the array
It converts the habit into JSON

questions.prompt: addHabit uses crypto.randomUUID() for the habit id. Why would using habits.length as the id be a bug?
options: length is a string, not a number
It would be noticeably slower to compute
React does not allow ids that are numbers
After a habit is deleted, lengths repeat — so two different habits could end up with the same id

questions.prompt: In the useEffect in App.tsx, what is the returned function for?
options: It is the cleanup function — React runs it before the effect runs again and when the component unmounts, so listeners don't pile up
It runs once before the very first render
It cancels the click event
It is the value the effect hands back to the parent component

questions.prompt: That effect's dependency array is [weekOffset]. What happens each time weekOffset changes?
options: Nothing — an effect only ever runs once
The component unmounts and remounts
The cleanup runs first to remove the old listener, then the effect body runs again and adds a fresh one
The effect body runs again but the cleanup never does

questions.prompt: If that dependency array were [] instead of [weekOffset], what would console.log(weekOffset) print after you clicked Next several times and then clicked the page?
options: The current weekOffset each time
undefined
It would throw an error
Always 0, because the handler captured the value from the first render and was never replaced

questions.prompt: If the dependency array were removed entirely — useEffect(() => { ... }) with no second argument — how often would the effect run?
options: Only once, after the first render
After every single render
Never
Only when the component unmounts

questions.prompt: useLocalStorage calls useState<T>(() => { ... }) — passing a function rather than a plain value. What does that achieve?
options: It is a lazy initializer — the localStorage read and JSON.parse run only on the first render instead of on every render
It makes the state update asynchronous
It is required syntax whenever useState is given a generic type
It prevents the state from ever changing

questions.prompt: useLocalStorage ends with return [storedValue, setStoredValue] as const. What is as const doing there?
options: Making the array read-only at runtime
Freezing the state value so it cannot be reassigned
Typing the return as a fixed tuple [T, setter] instead of a mixed array, so destructuring gives each variable the right type
Nothing — it could be removed with no effect

questions.prompt: The useEffect inside useLocalStorage has [storedValue, key] as its dependencies. When does it write to localStorage?
options: Only once, when the component mounts
After every render, unconditionally
Before the component renders
After any render in which storedValue or key changed

questions.prompt: Why does this app put habits in a Context instead of passing them down as props from App?
options: Context is faster than passing props
It avoids prop drilling — Header and HabitList read the habits directly instead of App threading them through every level
Props cannot hold arrays or functions
Context saves the data to a server

questions.prompt: In usehabit.ts the context is created as createContext<null | Context>(null). Why is null part of the type and used as the default value?
options: Because a component rendered outside HabitProvider would receive that default, so the type has to admit that possibility
Because TypeScript requires every context to allow null
Because context values are always null and stay null
To make every field inside the context optional

questions.prompt: useHabits() does if (habitContext == null) throw new Error("Null context"). What does that guard buy you?
options: It replaces the null with an empty context object
It gives a clear error if the hook is used outside HabitProvider, and it narrows the type so every caller can use the value without null-checking
It creates a new context on the fly
It only logs a warning to the console

questions.prompt: Every render of HabitProvider builds a brand-new object { habits, addHabit, toggleHabit, deleteHabit } as the context value. What is the consequence of that?
options: The context is torn down and rebuilt from scratch
The provider unmounts its children
localStorage gets cleared
Every component that calls useHabits re-renders

questions.prompt: What does type ButtonProps = { variant?: Variant } & ComponentProps<"button"> accomplish?
options: It replaces all the native button props with just variant
It adds an optional variant prop on top of every standard <button> prop, such as onClick, disabled and children
It makes variant a required prop
It converts the component into a plain div

questions.prompt: Given function Button({ variant = "primary", className, ...props }: ButtonProps), what does props contain inside the function body?
options: Every prop, including variant and className
Only onClick
All the remaining props except variant and className, which were pulled out by the destructuring
An empty object

questions.prompt: In Header.tsx you have format(visibleDates.at(-1)!, "MMM d"). What does .at(-1) return, and what does the ! mean?
options: The first element; ! is the logical NOT operator
The array's length; ! is required syntax after .at()
A shallow copy of the array; ! reverses it
The last element; ! is a non-null assertion telling TypeScript the value is not undefined

questions.prompt: What job does twMerge from tailwind-merge do in Button.tsx?
options: It merges Tailwind class strings and resolves conflicts, so a className passed into Button wins over the defaults
It compiles Tailwind CSS at build time
It minifies the class names for production
It converts Tailwind utilities into plain CSS rules

questions.prompt: In startOfWeek(week, { weekStartsOn: 1 }), what does weekStartsOn: 1 mean?
options: The week starts on Sunday
It shifts the week forward by one
It selects the first week of the year
The week starts on Monday

questions.prompt: In Header.tsx the Next button has disabled={visibleDates.some(d => isToday(d))}. What is the practical effect?
options: Next is disabled at weekends
Next is disabled while there are no habits yet
Next is disabled whenever the week on screen contains today, so you cannot browse into future weeks
Next is permanently disabled

questions.prompt: Trace getStreak. Today is Wednesday, and a habit's completions contains Wednesday and Tuesday but NOT Monday. What does it return?
Same getStreak function. Today is Wednesday. This time completions contains Tuesday and Monday, but today has NOT been completed yet. What does it return?
useLocalStorage passes a dateReviver to JSON.parse. What problem is that solving?
options: It compresses the stored JSON
JSON has no Date type, so saved dates come back as plain strings — the reviver turns matching ISO strings back into real Date objects
It encrypts whatever is written to localStorage
It sorts the completions by date

questions.prompt: What would actually break if you deleted dateReviver and just called JSON.parse(item)?
options: Nothing would change
localStorage would stop saving anything
All saved habits would be deleted on refresh
After a refresh, completions would hold strings instead of Dates, so the isSameDay comparisons — the day checkmarks and the streak — would stop working
